prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Sibanye Stillwater Ltd" (ticker SBSW), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SBSW", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Sibanye Stillwater Limited
result.industry: Precious metals mining (platinum group metals and gold), PGM recycling and battery metals
markets: Platinum group metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, ruthenium) from South African and US (Montana) mines
Gold from South African underground mines and tailings (including 50.1%-owned DRDGOLD)
PGM autocatalyst recycling (Columbus, Montana; Reldan in the US)
Lithium hydroxide project (Keliber, Finland) and chrome, nickel and silver by-products

mission.statement: Creating a better future for people and planet through our metals
mission.source: Company website (sibanyestillwater.com, About us), published as the company's purpose; vision: "To be a leader in creating shared value for all stakeholders"
mission.plain: Mine and recycle the metals the world needs in a way that leaves people and the planet better off.

about.plain: Sibanye-Stillwater digs platinum-type metals and gold out of deep mines in South Africa, and platinum-type metals out of mines in Montana in the US. It also recycles old car exhaust parts to recover the precious metals inside them. It reprocesses old mine waste in Australia to get zinc and is building a lithium business in Finland for car batteries. It sells the metals at world market prices.
about.customers: Car-parts makers, refiners, banks, metal traders and smelters buy its metals.
about.everyday: The platinum, palladium and rhodium it mines sit inside car catalytic converters that clean exhaust fumes, and its gold ends up in jewellery and gold bars.

money.plain: Platinum, palladium, rhodium and chrome from Rustenburg, Marikana and Kroondal (R60,883m of FY2025 revenue)
Gold from Driefontein, Kloof, Beatrix, Cooke and DRDGOLD tailings (R37,059m)
Precious metals recovered from used catalytic converters and scrap in the US (R20,865m)
Palladium and platinum from Stillwater and East Boulder (R6,718m)
Lithium for electric-car batteries; mining started in February 2026, refinery decision still pending

result.summary: Sibanye-Stillwater sells commodities at world prices, so it has no brand, switching-cost or network advantage and its profits swing with PGM and gold prices: revenue fell from R172,194m in 2021 to R112,129m in 2024 before recovering to R129,677m in 2025. Its real advantages are a cornered resource (large, long-life Bushveld PGM and Montana palladium ore bodies, in a market with few producers) and deep-level mining know-how, but its South African mines are relatively high-cost and labour-intensive.

pricingPower.evidence: It is a price taker: H1 2026 revenue jumped 64% to R89,977m mainly because the SA PGM basket price rose 67% and the gold price 35% while SA PGM output was flat at 831,307 4Eoz and gold output fell 2%; when PGM prices fell in 2023 it booked R47,454m of impairments and a R37,430m loss.

moats.evidence: Platinum, palladium and gold are sold on specification at market prices, so the Sibanye-Stillwater name earns no premium.
Refiners, banks and car-catalyst makers can buy identical metal from Valterra, Implats, Northam or Nornickel at no cost to switch.
More customers do not make its metal more valuable to other customers.

It is one of the largest PGM producers (1,724,778 4Eoz from SA PGM in 2025) but at an all-in sustaining cost of R24,193/4Eoz (US$1,353) and SA gold AISC of US$2,509/oz in 2025 it sits mid-to-high on the cost curve; scale helps share overheads but the conventional, labour-intensive mines are not low-cost.

Primary PGM supply is concentrated in a handful of producers in South Africa's Bushveld, Russia and Zimbabwe, and new deep-level mines take a decade and billions of rand to build, which limits new entry.
Its counter-cyclical acquisition strategy (Stillwater in 2017, Lonmin in 2019) and move into recycling and battery metals are moves any well-funded rival could copy.

Running ultra-deep gold mines and large Bushveld PGM shafts safely is rare know-how built over decades, and its Montana operations mine one of the world's few high-grade palladium reefs; safety lapses (6 fatalities in 2025, 3 in Q2 2026) show the difficulty.
It owns long-life mining rights on the Bushveld Complex (which hosts most of the world's platinum reserves) and the J-M Reef in Montana, the only significant US source of primary PGMs.

customers.evidence: Buyers (car-catalyst makers, refiners, banks and traders) purchase on price and specification, so loyalty is low, but demand for its metal is steady; it sells refined PGMs to customers in the USA, UK, EU, Canada and Japan and gold mainly to international and local banks.

talent.evidence: It is one of South Africa's largest mining employers and promotes from within (CEO Richard Stewart joined in 2014), but deep-level mining is dangerous, union relations are tense (a three-month gold wage strike in 2022) and it does not appear in major best-employer rankings.

product.evidence: Its metals are standard commodities identical to rivals'; the distinctive parts are a broad basket (platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, ruthenium plus gold) and a large autocatalyst recycling business (308,617 3Eoz fed at Columbus in 2025).

competitors.name: Valterra Platinum (formerly Anglo American Platinum)
competitors.note: World's largest primary PGM producer, with Mogalakwena and other Bushveld mines and refining in South Africa

competitors.name: Impala Platinum Holdings (Implats)
competitors.note: Bushveld PGM mines (Impala Rustenburg, Bafokeng), Zimbabwe (Zimplats) and Canada; direct rival in PGM supply

competitors.name: Northam Platinum Holdings
competitors.note: South African PGM producer (Zondereinde, Booysendal, Eland)

competitors.name: MMC Norilsk Nickel
competitors.note: Largest palladium producer, competing directly with Stillwater's palladium-heavy output

competitors.name: Harmony Gold Mining Company Limited
competitors.note: South Africa's largest gold producer, with deep-level mines and tailings retreatment next to Sibanye's

competitors.name: Gold Fields Limited
competitors.note: Former parent (Sibanye Gold was unbundled from Gold Fields in 2013); South Deep mine and global gold operations

competitors.name: AngloGold Ashanti plc
competitors.note: Global gold miner and former South African deep-level operator competing for capital and assets

competitors.name: African Rainbow Minerals
competitors.note: PGM interests (Two Rivers, Modikwa, Nkomati) in the Bushveld

competitors.name: Tharisa plc
competitors.note: Bushveld PGM and chrome producer, competing in PGMs and chrome by-product

competitors.name: Johnson Matthey
competitors.note: PGM refining, autocatalyst recycling and trading, competing with Sibanye's recycling business

competitors.name: Heraeus Precious Metals
competitors.note: Private German PGM recycler and refiner competing for spent autocatalysts

competitors.name: Umicore
competitors.note: Precious-metal recycling and battery materials, overlapping with recycling and the Keliber lithium strategy

competitors.name: Albemarle Corporation
competitors.note: Largest lithium producer, a future rival for Keliber's lithium hydroxide sales in Europe

marketShare.market: Global gold mine production (approximate estimate, assuming ~116Moz world output in 2025)

threats: Battery-electric cars need no catalytic converters, so faster EV adoption would cut demand for palladium and rhodium, its largest PGM revenue sources after platinum
PGM and gold price falls: the 2023 PGM price slump caused R47,454m of impairments and a R37,430m loss
High-cost, labour-intensive South African mines exposed to wage inflation, union action and Eskom power supply problems
Safety incidents (6 fatalities in 2025, 3 more in Q2 2026) that bring stoppages and regulatory scrutiny
Loss-making periods at the US PGM mines, which were restructured in 2024 and depend on the Section 45X production tax credit and a new labour agreement
Execution risk on new projects (Keliber lithium refinery, Burnstone gold, Mt Lyell copper) and weak lithium prices
Russian (Nornickel) palladium supply and PGM substitution or thrifting by car makers
Stronger rand, which lowers rand revenue from dollar-priced metals

ceo.name: Richard Stewart
ceo.background: Geologist with a PhD in geology from the University of the Witwatersrand; joined Sibanye in 2014, former group COO and chief regional officer for Southern Africa; earlier at Gold One and Goliath Gold

c1.evidence: Sibanye-Stillwater is a large producer in mature industries (PGM and gold mining), and its FY2025 revenue of R129,677m was below FY2021's R172,194m.

c2.evidence: Customers choose its metal on price and specification rather than brand or innovation; its edge is ownership of long-life Bushveld and Montana ore bodies, not anything customers would pay more for.

c3.evidence: Outside mining and investing circles few people know the name, and it is not the default leader: Valterra Platinum is the largest primary PGM producer and Nornickel the largest palladium producer.

c4.evidence: Its purpose, "Creating a better future for people and planet through our metals", is linked to green metals (PGMs for hydrogen, lithium, recycling), but management is judged mainly on returns and capital discipline.

c6.evidence: "South African miner, platinum, gold, cyclical, risky": the impression among investors is mixed, reflecting volatile profits, safety incidents and big swings in the share price.

c7.evidence: PGM and gold markets are large but not growing fast, and PGM autocatalyst demand is threatened by electric cars; hydrogen, recycling and battery metals offer a smaller secular tailwind.

c8.evidence: It has expanded into recycling (Reldan), zinc tailings (Century) and lithium (Keliber) and is developing Burnstone gold and Mt Lyell copper, but these are commodity extensions rather than new large markets.

m1.evidence: Richard Stewart has refocused the company on 'simplify, performance excellence, value-focused growth and disciplined capital allocation' rather than a bold new vision.

m2.evidence: Stewart is a hired professional CEO since 1 October 2025, not a founder; founding-era CEO Neal Froneman retired on 30 September 2025.

m4.evidence: There is no specific public evidence that Stewart's leadership style is servant-led; the company emphasises its iCARES values (innovation, commitment, accountability, respect, enabling, safety).

m5.evidence: Sibanye's culture is built around operating and acquiring mines, not inventing new products; it spends little on research and development.

m6.evidence: Stewart is a geologist with a Wits PhD who ran operations as group COO and chief regional officer for Southern Africa before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: There is no specific evidence either way beyond the company's stated purpose and community programmes; his tenure began only in October 2025.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech at a top university by Richard Stewart could be found.

m8b.evidence: Stewart has a low public profile compared with his outspoken predecessor Neal Froneman.

m9.evidence: As COO and regional head he oversaw operations through the 2023-24 PGM downturn; in his first full half as CEO (H1 2026) adjusted EBITDA more than doubled to R31,843m, largely on higher metal prices.

m10.evidence: Management cut costs and restructured shafts and the US PGM operations during the 2023-24 downturn, but the company is not known for frugality as a culture.

c10.evidence: Its PGMs clean car exhaust for millions of vehicles and its gold supports savings, but the products are commodities that rivals also supply.

p2.evidence: Mining ore kilometres underground in South Africa and Montana and refining PGMs is very hard, and the metals are important for cleaner cars, hydrogen and electronics.

f1.evidence: Revenue fell in 2022, 2023 and 2024 (R172,194m to R138,288m to R113,684m to R112,129m) before rising to R129,677m in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin (revenue less cost of sales) fell from 34.6% in 2020 to 24.6% in 2025, after dipping to 6.2% in 2024.

f3.evidence: At 30 June 2026 gross debt was R32,104m against cash of R22,386m (net debt R9,718m, 0.18x adjusted EBITDA), and equity was positive at R44,167m at end-2025.

f4.evidence: Profit swung from R30,622m in 2020 to losses of R37,430m (2023), R5,710m (2024) and R4,739m (2025), and operating cash flow fell from 2021 levels to R7,095m in 2023 before recovering to R21,407m in 2025.

v1.evidence: Its platinum, palladium and gold are identical to rivals' metal, so there is no product reason for anyone to prefer it.

v2.evidence: It does not appear in major best-employer rankings, and its mines carry safety risks (6 fatalities in 2025).

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, car makers and refiners would lose a large share of global PGM supply and prices would spike, and tens of thousands of South African mine workers and their communities would be hit, but other producers could eventually fill the gap.
